questions.question: How did the legacy Bridge let JavaScript and native code communicate?
options: By passing serialized JSON messages asynchronously between the JS and native threads, batched per frame
Through a shared memory buffer with no serialization
JavaScript compiled directly to native machine code
questions.explanation: The Bridge required every interaction to be serialized to JSON, sent across asynchronously, and deserialized on the receiving side.

questions.question: Why could high-frequency interactions like drag gestures or scroll-linked animations suffer under the old Bridge architecture?
options: The Bridge was only built for touch events, not gestures
Every frame of interaction required sending more serialized bridge messages, which added overhead and could cause visible jank
Gestures are not supported without the New Architecture at all
The Bridge only operated once per app launch
questions.explanation: The asynchronous, serialized, per-frame nature of bridge communication made rapid, continuous interactions especially costly compared to occasional, discrete ones.

questions.question: What does JSI fundamentally enable that the Bridge could not?
options: Running native code without any JavaScript
JavaScript holding a direct reference to a native object and calling its methods synchronously, without serialization or an async round-trip
Writing native UI in JavaScript syntax
Removing the need for a JavaScript engine entirely
questions.explanation: JSI replaces message-passing with direct, synchronous method calls between JS and native C++ objects.

questions.question: What do TurboModules and Fabric have in common?
options: They are unrelated systems that don't share any underlying mechanism
Both are New Architecture components built on JSI — TurboModules for native modules, Fabric for the UI renderer
They are both deprecated in favor of the Bridge
They only matter for Android, not iOS
questions.explanation: Both replace older Bridge-based mechanisms (legacy native modules and the old renderer) with JSI-powered, more direct communication with native code.
